I have been farming these nine mu for forty-five years. My old man taught me, and now my son helps me in the field. I never went to school, but I know this land and I know cotton.

Last year I planted hybrid cotton seeds — the kind that Old Wang from the east end of the village used. His cotton grew better than mine the year before, so I switched. The seeds come from the dealer in town. This year I will plant the same. One bag covers my nine mu.

For fertilizer, when I rotary till in April, I put one 50-kilogram bag of compound fertilizer per mu. That is nine bags for my whole field. Then when the cotton flowers in July, I top-dress with urea. I buy five bags of urea for the whole field — about half a bag per mu — and I split it into two times, once when the flowers open and once when the bolls start swelling. I do not know those science numbers, but that is what goes in the ground. I would rather put a little too much than risk small bolls. Losing yield is a disaster; wasting some fertilizer is just a cost.

Water comes from my well. I run the pump three times: right after planting so the seeds come up strong, once in July when the flowers open and it is hot, and once in August when the bolls are growing. Three times is what my neighbors do. Electricity costs money, so I do not water more than that.

Pests are the enemy. I spray five times. First when the seedlings are about a hand tall, then every two or three weeks through the summer. Last year I only sprayed four times and the worms got into some bolls. I will not make that mistake again.

I use the rotary tiller. Deep ploughing costs too much diesel. Rotary is fine, breaks up the soil good for cotton.

Last year I got about 500 jin of seed cotton per mu. This year if the weather is normal, I think I can get 560 jin per mu — that is 280 kg in your measuring.
